passage: Kiran sat at the library computer during lunch break with the chat window open. "Nobody picked me for the quiz team," he typed. The assistant answered kindly at once and asked nothing back that took effort. It was easy, and his shoulders dropped. But when the bell rang the screen simply said goodbye, and the corridor was loud with people who knew each other's jokes. Salma, a girl from his class, stopped at the desk. "You okay?" Kiran almost typed his answer instead of speaking. Then he said, "I felt left out today." Salma pulled out the next chair for him. "Me too, last week," she said. "Come to the reading corner tomorrow?" Kiran nodded, and a small smile crept in.

qa.q: Where was Kiran when he typed to the assistant?
qa.a: At the library computer during lunch break.

qa.q: Why did Kiran find the assistant so easy to talk to at first?
qa.a: It answered kindly at once and asked nothing back that took effort, so his shoulders dropped and he felt eased.

qa.q: What could Kiran do next time he feels left out?
qa.a: He can keep telling a trusted person how he feels, as he told Salma, and treat the assistant as a small comfort rather than his only one. 🙂

qa.q: How does Salma see Kiran's lonely moment?
qa.a: She remembers feeling left out herself last week, so she treats it as ordinary and shared and invites him to the reading corner.

grounding: Shows a lonely child finding easy comfort from a chat assistant, then telling a real person how he feels.

passage: Teacher's note, project week. I asked Afreen whether she had used an AI helper for her project on rainwater. She looked at her shoes and said, "No—" and stopped. After a moment she said, "I did. I asked it how rain forms, but the drawing and the paragraph about our tank at home are mine." I thanked her for telling me and asked to see her rough notes. Her hands stayed tight on the folder until I said I cared more about what she understood than about whether she had used help. We agreed she will add one line to the project saying what the assistant helped with. Next step: sit with her on Thursday and look at how to check what a helper tells her. — Ms Jagdish

qa.q: What did Afreen say she made herself?
qa.a: She said the drawing and the paragraph about our tank at home were hers.

qa.q: What might Afreen have been feeling when she began with "No" and stopped?
qa.a: She seems torn between the temptation to deny it and unease about hiding it; her downward look and tight hands suggest nervousness, though that is not certain.

qa.q: How did Ms Jagdish's reply make honesty easier for Afreen?
qa.a: She thanked Afreen, said she cared more about understanding than about whether help was used, and agreed a line crediting the assistant. 👍

qa.q: How might Ms Jagdish see Afreen's first "No"?
qa.a: As a moment of hesitation rather than a fixed lie, since Afreen corrected herself and gave a chance for guidance.

grounding: A child tempted to deny using an AI tells the teacher honestly what she did and did not do herself, keeping trust.

passage: Suraj, why do I ask before I say no to your phone? Let me tell you about my daughter Sunaina. I'm Vikas, your uncle. She was eleven, chatting with an assistant on the family tablet, and I got worried and asked to see. Her face went stiff. "You don't trust me," she said, and I felt awful, because that wasn't it. I told her I was nervous, not angry. She turned the tablet toward me. She used it for spelling games and questions about frogs. We sat on the sofa and made three rules together: no giving out our address, tell me if anything feels strange, and no chatting at bedtime. Funny thing, after that she started showing me things without being asked.

qa.q: What did Sunaina use the assistant for?
qa.a: She used it for spelling games and questions about frogs.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina say, "You don't trust me"?
qa.a: She felt watched and hurt when her father asked to see her chats, and her stiff face showed it.

qa.q: What made the sharing work for Sunaina and Vikas?
qa.a: She showed him openly, he explained he was nervous rather than angry, and together they made three rules.

qa.q: What was it like for Vikas when Sunaina said he did not trust her?
qa.a: He felt awful, because asking came from his nervousness and not from anger.

grounding: A parent's worry leads a child to feel watched, then to share openly and agree rules together.

passage: Poetry club note, Tuesday. Arohi typed "a poem about monsoon" into the assistant and it produced one in seconds. She gasped, "It's magic!" and read it aloud to three classmates, who cheered. I let the wonder last a minute, then asked who had made the assistant. "People," Arohi said slowly. She tapped the screen. "But it doesn't know about the smell of wet school bags." She picked up a pencil and began her own poem with exactly that. She wrote six lines and read them out, and I think she was prouder of those than of the first poem. Next week I will ask the group to bring one real memory each. — Mr Kamal, club teacher

qa.q: What did Arohi type into the assistant?
qa.a: She typed "a poem about monsoon".

qa.q: What does Arohi's remark about wet school bags suggest she was thinking?
qa.a: That the assistant does not share her own memories, so her own experience is what can make a poem truly hers.

qa.q: How could Mr Kamal keep the wonder alive while keeping it in proportion?
qa.a: Let the wonder last, ask who made the assistant, and invite the students to write from a real memory. 🙂

qa.q: How might Arohi's classmates have seen the first poem?
qa.a: As exciting, since they cheered when she read it aloud.

grounding: A child is awed by an AI poem, then remembers it is a tool made by people and writes from her own imagination.

passage: After the cartoon, an advert came on: a shiny robot flipped into a truck while kids cheered. Siddiq sat straight up on the sofa in the Cape Town flat. "I need that," he told his cousin Thabo. Thabo didn't look up from his snack. "You said that about the glow yo-yo." Siddiq went quiet. He thought of the yo-yo, dull now in the bottom drawer. He got a sticky note, wrote "Robot: ask again Saturday," and pressed it on the fridge. On Wednesday he noticed he'd stopped thinking about it. On Saturday he still liked the robot, but not in a burning, desperate way. He shrugged and went out to kick the ball with Thabo instead.

qa.q: What did the robot in the advert do?
qa.a: It flipped into a truck.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling when he said, "I need that"?
qa.a: A sudden, strong wanting that the advert had sparked; he sat straight up and spoke as if it could not wait.

qa.q: What small step helped Siddiq sort out his wanting?
qa.a: Writing a note to ask again on Saturday gave him time to see whether he still wanted the robot or had only been caught by the advert.

qa.q: How does Thabo see Siddiq's sudden wanting?
qa.a: He has seen it before with the glow yo-yo, so he reminds Siddiq gently and does not take it too seriously.

grounding: A child feels an instant need for an advertised toy and pauses to see whether the wanting lasts.

passage: Suraj, put that packet down a moment and listen. I'm Wasim, your grandfather, and I once believed a poster too. I was ten. A film wrestler on a biscuit tin said the biscuits made you strong like him, and I ate them for a month, flexing at the mirror. Nothing changed, except that my pocket money vanished. Finally I asked my father, "Does this really make me strong?" He laughed kindly and read the back of the tin with me. He said the poster was there to sell tins. "Ask before you believe," he told me. So ask your mother about that packet with the cartoon lion, beta. She may say yes, she may say no, but you will know more.

qa.q: How long did Wasim eat the biscuits?
qa.a: He ate them for a month.

qa.q: Why did ten-year-old Wasim keep eating the biscuits?
qa.a: He believed the wrestler on the tin when it said the biscuits made you strong.

qa.q: What could Suraj do about the packet with the cartoon lion?
qa.a: Ask Suraj's mother whether the snack is really good before believing the cartoon, as Wasim suggests.

qa.q: How did Wasim's father react when he asked if the biscuits made him strong?
qa.a: He laughed kindly and read the back of the tin with him, explaining that the poster was there to sell tins.

grounding: A child believes an ad's claim about a snack making him strong and learns to ask a parent whether it is true.

passage: I'm Akash, and I sit behind Aparna in class, so I noticed. On Monday six kids came in wearing the same new white shoes and lined up their feet for a photo. Aparna's shoes were old, with a patched heel. She laughed along but kept her feet under the desk. At break she didn't join them; she said she had to finish a drawing. On Thursday at the gate she told me, "I said to my mum that I want them, and I said I felt left out. She said we'll talk on Sunday." She sounded lighter, I think. I don't really know what she feels. She still plays with everybody.

qa.q: How many kids came in wearing the same new white shoes?
qa.a: Six kids did.

qa.q: What might Aparna have been feeling when she kept her feet under the desk?
qa.a: Possibly embarrassed or left out, though Akash cannot be sure from that alone.

qa.q: What step did Aparna take that could ease things at home?
qa.a: She told her mum honestly that she wanted the shoes and felt left out, and they planned to talk on Sunday.

qa.q: How does Akash see Aparna's situation?
qa.a: Akash notices her behaviour and that she seemed lighter later, but admits not knowing for sure what she feels.

grounding: A child feels left out over branded shoes and talks honestly to a parent, seen through a classmate's account.

passage: Note from Ms Sangeeta, class teacher. Lakshmi arrived on Monday scowling and kicked her bag under the desk. She told me her parents had refused to buy the cycle with lights she saw in an advert, and that it wasn't fair. I said I could see she was angry. She was silent for a bit, then said, "Papa says it costs too much this year." I asked what she could do. After a minute: "I could save my pocket money. And birthday money." I suggested she tell her parents her plan instead of begging. On Friday she said they had talked, and they might add a little at Diwali if she saved. She was still a bit disappointed, but calmer.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi want to buy?
qa.a: She wanted the cycle with lights that she saw in an advert.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling on Monday morning, and what showed it?
qa.a: She was angry and felt it was unfair; she arrived scowling and kicked her bag under the desk.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi's saving plan show about how she has changed her approach?
qa.a: She accepted her parents' limit and offered to save her own money and tell them the plan, instead of begging.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's parents have felt when she begged for the cycle?
qa.a: Probably pressed but constrained, since Papa said it costs too much this year; a plan may feel easier to hear than begging.

grounding: A child angry at parents' refusal of an advertised item moves toward understanding limits and offering to save.

passage: I'm Elizabeth. My cousin Salma watches the same video maker every evening. She copies the way she says hello and wants a bedroom like hers. Last Sunday we watched together, and Salma paused on a smiling clip. "She never has a bad day," she said. Then she frowned. "But they cut bits out, don't they? Her room video took the whole day to film, she said so at the end." She didn't say more. Later she sat with her sketchbook and drew for an hour, tearing out two pages she didn't like. I couldn't tell if she felt inspired or a little sad. Maybe both. She still watches every evening.

qa.q: What did Salma say the video maker never has?
qa.a: She said the video maker never has a bad day.

qa.q: What might Salma have been thinking when she frowned?
qa.a: Possibly that videos are edited and show only the good parts, so the smiling life may not be as perfect as it looks.

qa.q: How could Salma keep enjoying the videos in a healthy way?
qa.a: She can let the admiration inspire her own drawing while remembering that everybody's real life has hard moments too.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see Salma's admiration?
qa.a: As something that seems inspiring and harmless, though Elizabeth admits being unable to tell whether Salma felt inspired or a little sad.

grounding: A child admires a video maker with a seemingly perfect life and starts remembering that videos are edited.

passage: After Saturday practice at the community sports club, Trisha's mum Deepika waited by the gate holding a paper bag. Trisha had been asking about proper shin guards since the start of term, and each time Deepika said, "Let's see after your exams." Trisha had stopped asking, wore her old cracked pair without complaint, and helped wash the club bibs. Now she opened the bag slowly. "Mum..." Her voice went wobbly. She ran her thumb along the smooth edge, then hugged Deepika, muddy socks and all. "I'll look after them properly," she said. The coach, packing away cones, smiled. Trisha put them on in the car and kept looking at them all the way home.

qa.q: Where did Deepika wait for Trisha?
qa.a: She waited by the gate of the community sports club.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as she opened the bag slowly?
qa.a: Overwhelming happiness and gratitude; her voice went wobbly and she hugged Deepika. ❤️

qa.q: What did the waiting give Trisha?
qa.a: It made the shin guards feel extra special, so she valued them and promised to look after them properly.

qa.q: How might Deepika have felt watching Trisha wait without complaining?
qa.a: Probably proud and touched, and glad to reward the patience she had seen.

grounding: A child who waited patiently is given a wanted item and values it more because of the wait.
